seoTitle: Michigan Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL) Lawyer – Preterm Brain Injury
seoDescription: Your premature baby was diagnosed with PVL. What it is, cystic vs. diffuse, when the ultrasound should have been done, which steps before and after birth reduce it (steroids, magnesium, ventilation, blood pressure), and when a Michigan claim exists. Free review.
tagline: PVL is the brain injury of prematurity. Some of it is the price of being born early. Some of it was preventable. The NICU chart tells which.

c.v: Periventricular leukomalacia, PVL, is injury to the white matter of a baby’s brain in the area surrounding the fluid-filled ventricles. “Leuko” is white, “malacia” is softening: the nerve fibers that carry signals from the brain’s surface down to the body are damaged or die, and because the fibers controlling the legs run closest to the ventricles, the signature result is spastic diplegia, the stiff-legged form of cerebral palsy. PVL is the most common serious brain injury of premature infants and the leading cause of cerebral palsy in babies born early.

Michigan’s preterm birth rate was 10.7 percent in 2024, worse than the year before and worse than the national rate of 10.4 percent; in Detroit it was 16.6 percent. Of Michigan’s 99,420 births that year, more than 10,000 babies were born before 37 weeks, and the ones born before 32 weeks, the babies at real risk of PVL, spent weeks or months in a neonatal intensive care unit where every hour of their care was charted.

Not every case of PVL is anyone’s fault. A baby born at 25 weeks has a brain that is vulnerable to injury from the ordinary stresses of being outside the womb too soon, and some white matter injury occurs despite careful care. But medicine knows a great deal about what causes PVL and what reduces it. Steroids given to the mother before a preterm delivery, magnesium sulfate given to protect the baby’s brain, antibiotics and prompt delivery for an infected uterus, a ventilator that does not blow off too much carbon dioxide, blood pressure that is kept in range, and a cranial ultrasound done on schedule so the injury is found and the child is treated early: each of these is a standard of care, each is documented, and each is sometimes missed. This page explains what PVL is, how it is diagnosed, the steps before and after birth that reduce it, when a Michigan malpractice claim exists, and the deadline that runs to the child’s tenth birthday.

sections.heading: What PVL is, and the two forms it takes

c.v: Between about 23 and 32 weeks of gestation, the cells that will become the brain’s white matter, the pre-oligodendrocytes that insulate nerve fibers, are at their most vulnerable. They sit in a region with a poor blood supply, and they are damaged by two things above all: a shortage of oxygen and blood flow, and inflammation. When either happens, the white matter beside the ventricles is injured.

Widespread injury to the developing white matter without cysts; the ventricles enlarge as the surrounding tissue fails to grow
Often missed on ultrasound; seen on MRI at term-equivalent age as abnormal signal and reduced white matter volume
The common form today; associated with cerebral palsy, cognitive and learning disability, attention problems, and visual-processing impairment

The two frequently occur together, and a grade IV hemorrhage (bleeding into the brain tissue itself) causes white matter injury of its own. The cranial ultrasound report will say which the baby has.

The two interventions in the first rows matter most in litigation, because they are simple, cheap, and specifically recommended. A mother who arrived at a Michigan hospital at 28 weeks with contractions, was observed for a day, and delivered without ever receiving betamethasone or magnesium has a chart in which the omission is visible on a single page.

PVL does not announce itself. A premature infant with PVL may look no different in the NICU from one without it. The diagnosis comes from imaging, and the timing of the imaging is part of the standard of care.

items.v: through the soft spot is the screening test. The AAP recommends it for every infant born at or before 30 weeks: a first scan at 7 to 10 days, a repeat at 4 to 6 weeks because that is when cysts become visible, and a final scan at 36 to 40 weeks corrected age or before discharge. Infants born between 30 and 34 weeks are scanned if they had a complicated course.

c.v: The diagnosis matters legally in two ways. A baby who was never scanned, or scanned once at a week of age and declared normal, may have had PVL that went undiagnosed until cerebral palsy was obvious, delaying the early intervention that improves outcomes. And the imaging dates the injury: cysts seen at four weeks reflect an insult two to six weeks earlier, which places it in a specific window of the NICU course, or in labor, and lets the experts match it to what the chart shows was happening then.

The defense’s theme in every PVL case is that prematurity itself caused the injury and nothing could have changed it. The answer is specific: the omitted steroid or magnesium dose, the blood gas log showing hours of hypocarbia, the blood pressures that were charted and not treated, the fever that was not treated for twelve hours.

faqs.question: My baby was born at 26 weeks and has PVL. Isn’t that just what happens to very premature babies?

answer.v: Sometimes. White matter injury is a risk of extreme prematurity even with careful care. But the risk is reduced by specific, documented steps before and after birth: antenatal steroids, magnesium sulfate, infection control, ventilation that avoids low carbon dioxide, and blood pressure management. Whether those steps were taken is in the chart, and that is the question we answer.

faqs.question: What are “steroids” and “magnesium,” and why does it matter whether my doctor gave them?

answer.v: Betamethasone given to a mother expected to deliver between 24 and 34 weeks matures the baby’s lungs and reduces brain hemorrhage and death. Magnesium sulfate given before delivery under 32 weeks reduces the rate of cerebral palsy. Both are recommended by ACOG and both are routine. A mother who was in the hospital long enough to receive them and did not is entitled to ask why.

faqs.question: The NICU said the ultrasound at one week was normal. How does my baby have PVL?

answer.v: Because the cysts of PVL take two to six weeks to appear. That is why the AAP recommends a repeat scan at four to six weeks and another at term-equivalent age. If your baby was scanned only once, ask whether the later scans were done.

faqs.question: What is the difference between PVL and a brain bleed?

answer.v: A brain bleed (intraventricular hemorrhage) is bleeding into the ventricles, graded I through IV. PVL is injury to the white matter around the ventricles from poor blood flow or inflammation. They often occur together, and the ultrasound report will describe both.

faqs.question: Will my child have cerebral palsy?

answer.v: PVL is the most common cause of cerebral palsy in premature infants, and cystic PVL in particular is strongly associated with spastic diplegia. Diffuse injury has a wider range of outcomes, including learning and attention problems without motor disability. Your child’s neurologist and the term-equivalent MRI are the best guide.

The child’s claim is open until the tenth birthday for an injury before age eight. The parents’ own claims run two years. A university hospital requires notice within six months of the event. The 182-day notice of intent precedes every suit, and records must be requested before the hospital’s seven-year retention period ends.

faqs.question: We were at a small hospital and the baby was transferred after birth. Does that matter?

answer.v: It can. The standard of care favors transferring the mother before delivery to a hospital with a Level III or IV NICU when preterm delivery is expected and transfer is safe. A baby born at 28 weeks at a hospital without a NICU and transported afterward has spent his most vulnerable hours without the care he needed.

faqs.question: What is a PVL case worth?

answer.v: It depends on the extent of the injury and what the child will need. Economic damages are uncapped; the life care plan for a child with cerebral palsy from PVL is commonly in the millions. Non-economic damages are capped at $596,400 or $1,065,000 for 2026. We do not quote figures before the records and a life care plan are in hand.
